content:
Giv (also written Gew, Giw) is one of the foremost Iranian champions in Ferdowsi’s Shahnameh, a pillar of the House of Gudarz and a paragon of loyalty and endurance. He serves chiefly under the Kayanian kings Kay Kavus and Kay Khosrow.

Who he is
- Lineage and clan:
  - Father: Gudarz (Gudârz), patriarch of a powerful warrior clan that supplies many of Iran’s commanders and heroes.
  - Siblings/kin: Often grouped with other Gudarzids (e.g., Rohham/Gostaham and others) who fight on Iran’s side in the Iran–Turan wars.
  - Wife (in later epics and some traditions): Banu Goshasp, the formidable daughter of Rostam. Their marriage is central in the Banu Goshasp-Nameh.
  - Son: Bijan, the hero of the famous romance “Bijan and Manijeh.”
- Rank and role: A leading pahlavan (champion) and field commander, frequently at the heart of Iran’s campaigns against Turan. He is both a battlefield hero and a trusted royal retainer.

Signature episodes and deeds
- The seven-year quest for Kay Khosrow:
  - After the martyrdom of Siyavash in Turan, Gudarz dreams that Siyavash’s son lives. Giv volunteers for a perilous mission to find and bring back the child heir.
  - He spends years in Turan—often given as seven—searching relentlessly, evading Afrasiyab’s agents, and ultimately locating Farangis (Siyavash’s widow) and the young Kay Khosrow.
  - He escorts them safely to Iran, a deed that preserves the Kayanian line and changes the course of the epic. This is Giv’s defining act and the one most celebrated in Persian miniature and storytelling.
- Wars of Iran and Turan under Kay Kavus and Kay Khosrow:
  - Giv leads divisions, champions single combats, and is central to many campaigns against Afrasiyab’s forces. He stands as a principal counterpart to Turanian champions and a stalwart of the Iranian army (often alongside his father Gudarz, and parallel to, sometimes in tension with, the command of Tus).
- The story of Bijan and Manijeh:
  - As Bijan’s father, Giv is deeply tied to this romance-adventure. When Bijan is trapped by Afrasiyab (with the complicity and cowardice of Gorgin), Giv is distraught. Rostam’s covert expedition rescues Bijan, and Giv plays a prominent role in the aftermath at court; he is stern with Gorgin but accedes to Bijan’s plea for clemency.
- The end with Kay Khosrow:
  - When Kay Khosrow withdraws from the world, he warns the heroes not to follow him into the mountains. Several loyal champions ignore the warning, pursue him, and are caught in a supernatural blizzard. Giv is among those who perish—an ending that underlines his unwavering loyalty even to the point of death.

Character and symbolism
- Embodiment of fidelity: Giv is the Shahnameh’s model of steadfast service to king and country—quietly relentless, dutiful, and self-sacrificing.
- Protector of the royal farr (divine glory): By rescuing Kay Khosrow, he ensures the continuance of legitimate, divinely sanctioned kingship in Iran.
- House of Gudarz ideal: As Gudarz’s foremost son, he personifies the clan’s virtues—courage, counsel, and continuity across generations (grandfather Gudarz, father Giv, son Bijan).

Family and relationships in more detail
- Spouse: Banu Goshasp (in later heroic romances, especially Banu Goshasp-Nameh). Their marriage—after a bout of trial by combat, as is common in these epics—links the houses of Gudarz and Zabul (Rostam’s line).
- Child: Bijan, whose tale with Manijeh (Afrasiyab’s daughter) is one of the Shahnameh’s most beloved narratives, mixing courtly love with espionage and rescue.

Names and earlier tradition
- Name forms: Giv, Gew, Giw (Persian); Middle Persian/Pahlavi: Wēw/Gēw; often “Giv son of Gudarz.”
- Pre-Islamic echoes: Members of the Gudarz clan (including a figure corresponding to Giv) appear in Middle Persian literature and Zoroastrian tradition, suggesting that Ferdowsi is drawing on deep, older heroic cycles in which the Gudarzids are prominent Iranian champions.

In art and later literature
- Visual depictions: Persian miniatures frequently show Giv ferrying Farangis and the child Kay Khosrow across the Oxus (Jihun) or guiding them through Turan, as well as standing in the ranks of Iran’s champions in war scenes.
- Later epics: Besides the Shahnameh, Giv figures in subsidiary epics and romances (e.g., Banu Goshasp-Nameh), which elaborate his marriage and clan ties.

How to think of Giv among Shahnameh’s heroes
- Rostam is unmatched in sheer might and mythic stature; Tus often represents command authority and royal lineage; Gudarz embodies elder statesmanship. Giv is the exemplar of tireless, loyal action—the hero who does the hard, unglamorous, sustained work that saves a dynasty.
- His legacy runs through Bijan and the posterity of the Gudarzids, anchoring one of the Shahnameh’s major family lines across reigns and wars.

Fate
- Dies in the snowstorm after following Kay Khosrow’s final departure, one of the heroes who vanish with their king’s withdrawal—an ending that crowns a life of devoted service with a bittersweet, near-sacral loyalty.

If you want, I can list specific cantos/episodes and standard English translations where Giv’s major scenes appear for easier reading.
